svg.font-family: Inter, Segoe UI, Helvetica, Arial, sans-serif
svg.title: Figure 1. Three channels data leaves an app by, and least privilege only closes one
svg.desc: Three routes by which data leaves a mobile application. The first is the permission you granted, which the standard advice covers and which least privilege genuinely closes. The second is the third party code inside the application, which inherits every permission the application holds, so one grant is handed to several companies at once. The third is the advertising request, which needs no permission at all: the bid request carries a device identifier and network address, every bidder receives it whether or not it wins, and location data brokers harvest from that stream. A band below explains that each channel needs a different control, and that minimising permissions addresses only the first.
svg.text: Figure 1: Three Channels, and Least Privilege Closes One
The standard model is that a permission granted is data given away. That is true, and it is about a third of the picture.
the channel every guide is about

g.text: You tapped allow. The application can
now read that thing, within the scope
you granted, until you revoke it.
Least privilege genuinely closes this.
Deny what makes no sense, reduce the
scope of what does, and revoke what you
stopped using. It works.
And it is visible.
Both platforms show you which
applications hold which permissions and
when each was last used.
Visible, controllable, and reversible,
which is exactly why it gets all the
attention. Do the work here. It is real.
Then read the other two panels.

svg.text: you granted one company, and got several

g.text: A modern application is assembled from
third party components: analytics,
crash reporting, advertising, payments.
Each one runs inside the app, so each
one inherits every permission the app
holds. The system cannot tell them apart.
When you grant location to a game, you
grant it to the game and to whichever
advertising components it ships with.
Least privilege limits the damage here
but does not close the channel.
The control is choosing applications with
fewer components, which is a research
task rather than a settings task.
Section 4 covers how to check.

svg.text: no permission required, and none is asked for

g.text: To show an advert, the app sends a bid
request to an exchange. That request
carries a device identifier, a network
address, and often a location field.
Every bidder receives it, whether or
not they win. Anyone who can register
as a buyer sees the stream.
A location broker breached in January
2025 was tracking over a billion devices.
Researchers named more than three thousand
applications in the leaked data, including
games and dating applications.
Least privilege does not touch this at
all, because nothing was ever granted.
A regulator found one broker sourced

svg.text: about 60 percent of its data this way.
Each channel needs a different control, and only the first one is a settings screen

g.text: Channel one: permissions. Deny, reduce scope, revoke. Free, fast, effective, and covered in Section 5. This is the part the standard advice gets right.
Channel two: components. Choose differently. Fewer applications, open source where it exists, the website instead of the app. Deleting an app closes it completely.
Channel three: the bidstream. Reset or disable the advertising identifier, and block at the network. Neither is complete, and deleting the app is again the only full answer.

svg.text: Notice what appears in two of the three rows: removing an application is the only control that closes every channel at once.
Which is why the most effective item in this lesson is not a permission setting. It is the count of applications on your phone.
And why "I denied location, so it cannot know where I am" is a reasonable belief that the third panel makes false.
